PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Inflammation (ac:
Overview

Inflammation is the tissue response to injury/infection. The histology tells you whether it is acute (rapid, neutrophils) or chronic (persistent, mononuclear cells + repair).

🔬 Image slot — acute inflammation (neutrophils) vs chronic (lymphocytes/plasma cells/macrophages)
AcuteChronic
Onset/durationRapid, shortSlow, prolonged
Key cellsNeutrophilsLymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages
VascularVasodilation, increased permeability → exudate/oedemaAngiogenesis
TissueLittle; may resolveTissue destruction + fibrosis
Cardinal signs: rubor, calor, tumor, dolor, functio laesa. Acute may resolve, form an abscess/pus, or become chronic.
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • Acute = neutrophils (vasodilation, permeability, exudate); chronic = lymphocytes/plasma cells/macrophages + fibrosis.
  • Pus = neutrophils + debris (abscess); granuloma = a special chronic pattern.
  • Outcomes of acute inflammation: resolution, abscess, or chronicity.
PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granuloma Format:
Overview

A granuloma is a focal collection of activated epithelioid macrophages, a special pattern of chronic inflammation for hard-to-clear agents.

🔬 Image slot — granuloma with epithelioid macrophages, a multinucleate giant cell and a lymphocyte rim
  • Epithelioid macrophages (elongated, pink, epithelial-like) ± multinucleate giant cells (Langhans type), surrounded by lymphocytes
  • Caseating (central cheesy necrosis) → classically TB (also fungi); non-caseating → sarcoidosis, Crohn's, foreign body
  • Driven by T-helper cells & cytokines (IFN-γ, TNF) — a type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity response
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • Granuloma = epithelioid macrophages ± giant cells + lymphocyte rim.
  • Caseating → TB; non-caseating → sarcoidosis / Crohn's / foreign body.
  • Type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity; driven by IFN-γ / TNF (anti-TNF drugs risk TB reactivation).
PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell Death (apop:
Overview — Two Ways Cells Die
🔬 Image slot — apoptotic bodies vs coagulative necrosis
ApoptosisNecrosis
NatureProgrammed, regulated ('cell suicide')Unregulated (injury/ischaemia/toxin)
ScaleSingle cellsGroups of cells
CellShrinks; membrane intact → apoptotic bodiesSwells → membrane ruptures → contents leak
InflammationNoneYes (leaked contents)
NucleusCondensation, fragmentationPyknosis → karyorrhexis → karyolysis
Patterns of Necrosis ⭐
Coagulative — architecture preserved ('ghost cells'); most solid organs after ischaemia (e.g. MI)
Liquefactive — digested to liquid; brain infarcts & abscesses
Caseous — cheesy; TB
Fat — saponification; acute pancreatitis
Fibrinoid — pink fibrin-like in vessel walls; vasculitis/malignant HTN
Gangrenous — clinical term (limb; dry/wet)
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • Apoptosis = single cells, shrink, no inflammation, apoptotic bodies; necrosis = cell swelling + rupture + inflammation.
  • Necrosis patterns: coagulative (ischaemia/MI), liquefactive (brain/abscess), caseous (TB), fat (pancreatitis), fibrinoid (vasculitis).
  • Nuclear changes in necrosis: pyknosis → karyorrhexis → karyolysis.
PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neoplasia (benig:
Overview

A neoplasm is an abnormal, autonomous, excessive tissue growth. The histology decides benign vs malignant.

🔬 Image slot — well-differentiated benign tumour vs pleomorphic invasive malignant tumour
FeatureBenignMalignant
DifferentiationWell differentiated (resembles origin)Often poor (anaplasia)
BorderCircumscribed / encapsulatedInvasive, irregular
GrowthSlow; few, normal mitosesRapid; many, abnormal mitoses
NucleiUniformPleomorphic, hyperchromatic, high N:C ratio
MetastasisNoYes (the definitive malignant feature)
Naming: benign = '-oma' (adenoma, lipoma); malignant epithelial = carcinoma; malignant mesenchymal = sarcoma. Grade = differentiation; stage = spread (TNM).
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • Malignant hallmarks: invasion, metastasis, anaplasia, pleomorphism, abnormal mitoses.
  • Metastasis = the definitive proof of malignancy.
  • Nomenclature: carcinoma (epithelial), sarcoma (mesenchymal); grade = differentiation, stage = spread (TNM).
PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metaplasia & Dys:
Overview — Adaptation vs Pre-cancer
🔬 Image slot — Barrett's metaplasia and cervical dysplasia (CIN) examples
Metaplasia
  • Reversible replacement of one mature cell type by another, better suited to a stress
  • e.g. Barrett's (squamous→columnar, reflux); bronchial ciliated→squamous (smoking)
Dysplasia
  • Disordered, atypical growth — loss of maturation/architecture, nuclear atypia, mitoses; pre-malignant
  • Graded low→high; still within the basement membrane
Progression: normal → metaplasia → dysplasia → carcinoma in situ → invasive carcinoma. Carcinoma in situ = full-thickness dysplasia that has not breached the basement membrane.
Other Adaptations (for contrast)
Hyperplasia = ↑ cell number
Hypertrophy = ↑ cell size
Atrophy = ↓ size/number
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • Metaplasia = reversible cell-type switch (adaptive); dysplasia = pre-malignant atypia (still above the basement membrane).
  • Sequence: metaplasia → dysplasia → carcinoma in situ → invasive carcinoma.
  • Carcinoma in situ = full-thickness dysplasia, basement membrane intact.
PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibrosis & Repai:
Overview — Regeneration vs Scarring

Tissues heal either by regeneration (restoring normal tissue) or by repair with a fibrous scar — determined by the tissue's regenerative capacity and the extent of damage.

🔬 Image slot — granulation tissue with new capillaries, fibroblasts and inflammatory cells
  • Labile (skin, gut) & stable (liver) tissues can regenerate; permanent tissues (neurons, cardiac muscle) heal by scar
  • Granulation tissue = new capillaries + fibroblasts + inflammatory cells — the building block of repair
  • Fibroblasts lay down collagen (type III → remodelled to type I); myofibroblasts contract the wound
  • Healing by primary (clean apposed edges) vs secondary intention (large defect, more granulation/contraction)
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Organ fibrosis
Chronic injury → excess collagen (cirrhosis, pulmonary fibrosis) → loss of function.
Keloid
Excessive scar collagen beyond the wound margins.
Poor healing
Infection, ischaemia, diabetes, malnutrition (vitamin C).
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • Labile/stable tissues regenerate; permanent tissues (neurons, cardiac muscle) scar.
  • Granulation tissue = new capillaries + fibroblasts + inflammatory cells.
  • Collagen: type III (early) → remodelled to type I; myofibroblasts contract the wound.
  • Keloid = excess scar; fibrosis of organs → loss of function (cirrhosis, lung fibrosis).
PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascular Patholo:
Atherosclerosis

A chronic disease of the intima of large/medium arteries, building an atheromatous (fibrofatty) plaque.

🔬 Image slot — atherosclerotic plaque with lipid core, foam cells and a fibrous cap
  • Endothelial injury → LDL enters & is oxidised → macrophages ingest it → foam cells → fatty streak
  • Mature plaque = a lipid/necrotic core under a fibrous cap (smooth muscle + collagen)
  • Complications: plaque rupture → thrombosis (MI, stroke), stenosis, aneurysm, embolism
Thrombosis (Virchow's Triad)
Endothelial injury (e.g. plaque, arteries)
Stasis / turbulent flow (e.g. veins, AF)
Hypercoagulability
  • Lines of Zahn (alternating pale platelet/fibrin and dark red-cell layers) indicate a thrombus formed in flowing blood (ante-mortem)
  • Fate: propagation, embolism, dissolution, organisation/recanalisation
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • Atherosclerosis = intimal fibrofatty plaque: lipid/necrotic core + fibrous cap; foam cells. Rupture → thrombosis.
  • Thrombosis: Virchow's triad = endothelial injury + stasis + hypercoagulability.
  • Lines of Zahn = ante-mortem thrombus; a detached thrombus = embolus.
PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Common Tumour Hi:
Overview — Naming a Carcinoma by Its Pattern

Carcinomas are named by the epithelium they recapitulate — recognising the pattern names the tumour and often points to the origin.

🔬 Image slot — adenocarcinoma (glands), SCC (keratin pearls) and urothelial carcinoma side by side
TumourPatternTypical sites
AdenocarcinomaGland/duct formation ± mucin (signet-ring cells if intracellular mucin)Colon, breast, lung, prostate, pancreas, stomach
Squamous cell carcinomaKeratin pearls + intercellular bridges (desmosomes)Skin, lung, head & neck, oesophagus, cervix
Urothelial (transitional cell) carcinomaPapillary/flat urothelium with atypiaBladder, ureter, renal pelvis
IHC confirms lineage when a tumour is poorly differentiated (e.g. cytokeratin = carcinoma; specific markers localise the primary).
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • Adenocarcinoma = glands + mucin (signet-ring = intracellular mucin).
  • SCC = keratin pearls + intercellular bridges.
  • Urothelial (transitional) carcinoma = bladder/ureter; painless haematuria.
  • Poorly differentiated tumours → use IHC (cytokeratin etc.) to establish lineage/origin.
